## Overview

In this chapter, engineering for equity, we will explore the responsibilities
of designing products for a broad base of users. Our chapter explores how
embracing diversity can design systems that work for everyone and avoid
creating a harmful environment for users. Engineering for equity exists because
understanding the impact that software engineering has on underrepresented
people and diverse societies is something being researched and understood
today. Google is currently learning how to engineer products that empower and
respect all of their users. To make more equitable products, we have to
evaluate our own failures and encourage growth toward a more equitable future.

### Bias Is the Default

Everyone has biases that are often exhibited as unconscious bias, which
enforces existing stereotypes on people unintentionally. Unconscious bias is
more difficult of an act to mitigate than intentional acts of exclusion because
we might not even recognize our own bias when trying to do the right thing.
Google has failed to represent all users equitably in all of its products due
to these biases. Due to this failure, in 2015 there was a case study conducted
on Google missing the mark on racial inclusion.

Jacky Alciné recognized that Google's recognition algorithms in Google Photos
were recognizing and classifying his black friends as "gorillas." Google did
not respond to these mistakes immediately and did not completely address them
either. There were several things that caused this huge failure for Google.

1. Image recognition algorithms depend on being supplied with a "proper" or
complete data set.
   - The photo data that was fed to Google's image recognition algorithm was
   incomplete, this resulted in the data not representing the entire populace.
2. Google did not have much black representation, which affected decisions.
   - The unconscious bias of Google led to a subjective design in their
   algorithms and collection of datasets. This left a more representative
   product on the table.
3. Google's target market for image recognition did not include
underrepresented groups.
   - Google's tests did not catch the mistakes that the users did, which in
   turn embarrassed Google and harmed their users.

As late as 2018, Google had still not completely addressed the underlying
problem in its image recognition.

Other technology from Google faced similar failures just as the image
recognition did. Autocomplete can return offensive or racist results, Google's
ad system can be manipulated to show racist and offensive ads. YouTube can let
hate speech slip through the cracks even though it is outlawed on the platform.
In these cases, the technology itself is not to blame they were not designed to
target users or discriminate, but the unconscious bias of Google's programmers
resulted in a product that was not resilient enough to exclude these things and
returned results that harmed users. This led to decreased user trust and
engagement with the company from user bases that were harmed by these
exclusions.

### Understanding the Need for Diversity

To understand the need for diversity, we have to first disrupt the computer
science degree myth. This myth is that because a person has a computer science
degree or work experience, they have all the skills they need to be an
exceptional engineer. The degree is a necessary foundation, but the degree
alone does not make someone an engineer. We also have to disrupt the idea that
only people with degrees can design and build products. Most programmers do
have a degree and are successful at building code, establishing theories of
change, and applying methods for problem solving. This approach is not
inclusive and equitable engineering. Engineers need to understand the
population demographics of all users and focus on people who are different from
themselves. Engineering teams need to build in representation of their existing
and future users. If there is not diverse representation in a team of engineers
they need to learn how to build for all users.

### Building Multicultural Capacity

Exceptional engineers need more than technical skill. They also need the
perception to understand how a product can advantage one group while
disadvantaging another, and when a feature should be delayed or rejected
because its possible harms have not been addressed. This requires building
multicultural capacity: learning about the different communities affected by a
product, seeking perspectives beyond our own experiences, and continuing to
develop our understanding of race, gender, ability, age, culture, and
socioeconomic status.

This responsibility cannot fall on one person alone. Engineering teams should
include perspectives that reflect their current and future users, while
organizations should provide ongoing, multidisciplinary professional
development. When a team lacks representation, engineers can still improve
their work by researching the people most likely to be excluded, involving
community members and subject-matter experts, and testing the most difficult
use cases first. Designing with the users who face the greatest barriers often
creates a better experience for everyone.

### Making Diversity Actionable

Making diversity actionable means turning good intentions into measurable
responsibility. Leaders should examine whether candidate pools, hiring
decisions, opportunities for advancement, and retention outcomes are equitable
instead of assuming that a policy is effective because it has inclusive goals.
Teams should also measure product outcomes across different user groups and
investigate disparities when they appear. These steps make equity part of the
engineering process rather than an issue considered only after harm occurs.

Progress also depends on accountability. Managers can review whether candidate
slates are representative, distribute growth opportunities fairly, and create
psychological safety for people from underrepresented groups. Engineers can
question processes that rely on incomplete data or narrow definitions of a
successful user. Together, these actions help organizations move from building
for everyone in theory to building with everyone in practice.

### Rejecting Singular Approaches

One of the main statements that you as a software engineer should hold close
is: "If we want to drive change and increase representation, we need to
evaluate whether we’re creating an ecosystem in which all aspiring engineers
and other technology professionals can thrive." We need to stay aware of the
fact that the software engineering field is not a monolith, and that there are
many different ways to approach problems.

We need to be open to new ideas and perspectives, and we need to be willing to
challenge our own assumptions. One common methodology is to build for the
majority use case first, leaving improvements and features that address edge
cases for later. This approach gives users who are not part of the majority use
case a subpar experience, and it can be frustrating for them to have to wait
for improvements that address their needs. We need to be willing to challenge
this approach and to build for all users from the start.

### Challenging Established Processes

A case at Google was evaluated for equity implications. Multiple engineering
teams got together to try to build a new feature, a global hiring requisition
system. Their main line of communication was the feedback from what would be
the main users of this new feature, recruiters. The recruiters main focus was
to minimize wasted time when it comes to hiring. One of the main features they
wanted added was the ability to highlight performance ratings as soon as
interest was expressed in a job by an internal transfer. This raised some
questions by another engineer:

- Are developmental assessments a predictive measure of performance?
- Are the performance assessments being presented to prospective managers free
of individual bias?
- Are performance assessment scores standardized across organizations?

If you answered "no" to any of these questions, then this new feature could
drive inequitable, and therefore potentially harmful, results.

After seeing the potential for inequitable results, a study was conducted in
which those with a lower performance rating were discovered to have a higher
likelihood of overcoming the poor rating if they found a new team. These
results showed that while ratings are important, they are only indicative of a
person's performance at that moment in time, and that they are not a predictive
measure of future performance.

### Values versus Outcomes

Despite a strong commitment, heavy investments, and inclusive core values,
Google continuously misses its goal of building a hiring workforce that
represents its global user base. The issue does not arise within company values
or intentions, but rather in how policies are applied and practiced at the
implementation level. Feedback is easy to gather when you rely on those
familiar, but do not consider those that you may not have reached yet.

How can we ensure that our values are reflected in our outcomes?

1. Take a hard look in the mirror.
   - True inclusivity requires fixing implementation failures and breaking old
   habits, rather than relying solely on good intentions or company values.
2. Don’t build for everyone. Build with everyone.
   - To build universally accessible technology, products must be designed with
   diverse communities, highlighting the most vulnerable populations, rather
   than assuming their needs.
3. Design for the user who will have the most difficulty using your product.
   - Don’t trade equity for short-term velocity.
   - Prioritizing and solving for the users who face the greatest barriers
   automatically improves the overall product experience for everyone.
4. Don’t assume equity; measure equity throughout your systems.
   - Keep in mind that even those who make decisions can also be under-educated
   and subject others to bias. Companies must be sure to continuously measure
   equity across all systems and collaborate with teams and individuals who are
   subject matter experts to expose and mitigate implicit biases.
5. Change is possible.
   - Overcoming modern, overwhelming digital challenges requires a fundamental
   willingness to abandon outdated, failing approaches in favor of continuous
   self-change.

### Pushing Forward

The path to equity will never be easy. Although we not only can but we should
transition from simply creating tools to growing our understanding of how what
we are producing will impact others. We should challenge our education,
influence our own teams and managers, and do comprehensive user research. As
future engineers ourselves we should focus first on the users who are most
impacted by bias and discrimination. It is possible together to accelerate
progress to a more inclusive engineering environment by owning up to our own
failures and make changes that push everyone forward without creating products
and environments that ignore underrepresented groups. This is not something
that can be done alone we all have to work together to produce these effects
and create products for not only ourselves and our peers but for those who
constantly face discrimination in the products that they use today.
